Why are property taxes based on unrealized gain - allleged (not realized) house value???? 😮😮😮😮

Because property taxes are not based on the unrealized gain but as a wealth and service tax on the assessed value of property.  Property taxes are not based on the gains, but the current assessed value.  So for example if you bought the house for $1M and it dropped in price ot $800k there  is no -$200k capital loss, you still owe property taxes, just now on an assessed value of $800k.  

[Aside] Is this somewhat word play?  Yes!  But that's the difference and the reason.  WA state passed an income tax in 2026, it's going to the voters to be possibly repealed and to the state supreme court (the state constitution states income is property and all property taxes need to be uniform and no more than 1%).  HOWEVER, the state is claiming that they did not create an income tax, but an excise tax.  It's a tax on the privilege and process of earning over $1M.  They tested the waters previous with a state capital gains tax which is also NOT a tax on income, but an excise tax on the privilege of earning and collecting your long term capital gains :)

Folks, I just wanted to add onto this. Youre not always going to be taxed at your own tax rate when you sell stocks.

There is something called “Short-Term Capital Gains” and “Long-Term Capital Gains” taxes. Short term means you held it for less than one year before selling, and you are taxed at your ordinary Income tax levels, but there is also Long-Term, which means you held it for at least one year, and you will be taxed at three different levels on a tier basis. The first tier, youre taxed at 0%, and then the next tier at 15%, and then lastly, all amounts above the previous tier at 20% max.

Bottom line is, it’s better to just hold your stocks for at least a year before you sell. This applies to Taxable accounts only. Your Retirement Accounts with a tax-deferred treatment won’t matter, as you’re only going to be taxed when you take distributions out of your retirement accounts.

that was the basics. for those that just started day trading and want to trade full time. you can apply for Trader Tax Status. then elect section 475 (mark to market accounting). this removes the $3k limit on losses and allows wash sales (buying the same stock immediately after selling for a loss). no 30 day limits to repurchase. also, you can deduct home office expenses. also note that mark to market accounting treats unrealized gains/losses as realized gains/losses and resets the cost basis of your unsold stocks at the end of the year.

trading in your brokerage is not the same as trading in your IRA/ROTH. you don't want to use tax loss harvesting in your retirement fund. there is no advantage. just DCA (dollar cost average) when the market dips.

How Stock Losses Work

• Short-Term Losses (Held 1 Year or Less): You can sell a stock immediately after buying it and claim a short-term capital loss.
• Long-Term Losses (Held More Than 1 Year): If you hold the stock for more than 12 months before selling it at a loss, it is classified as a long-term capital loss.
• Netting Losses: Capital losses must first be used to offset capital gains of the same type (short-term against short-term, long-term against long-term). If you have leftover net losses, you can use them to offset the other type of gain
